tip.title: Vous désirez ? Et avec ceci ?
tip.body: Market sellers use a few set phrases: Vous désirez ? (What would you like?), Et avec ceci ? (Anything else?) and Ce sera tout ? (Will that be all?). Prices are given per kilo: trois euros le kilo. In kilo the k sounds like an English k, and in ceci both c's sound like s.

tip.title: Il nous faut … and plus de …
tip.body: Il me faut (I need) and il nous faut (we need) are everyday ways to make a shopping list; on a besoin de works too. Il n'y a plus de … means there's no … left. Listen to the f in œuf: un œuf has a sounded f, but in des œufs the f is silent and you hear a liaison: des‿œufs ("day-zuh").

lessons.title: At the cheese counter
lessons.goal: Ask for slices, pieces and grams.

tip.title: Une tranche, un morceau, cent grammes
tip.body: At the deli or cheese counter you ask for une tranche (a slice), un morceau (a piece) or a weight in grams: deux cents grammes. After any quantity, French simply uses de: quatre tranches de jambon. The seller often holds the knife over the cheese and asks Comme ça ? (This much?) — answer Un peu plus or Un peu moins. In grammes the final -es is silent: "gram".

lessons.title: du, de la, des — and de
lessons.goal: Use the partitive, and de after quantities and negation.

tip.title: "Some" has to be said
tip.body: Where English says "some" or nothing at all (I'm buying bread), French needs a partitive article: du pain (masculine), de la confiture (feminine), de l'eau (before a vowel or mute h), des pommes (plural). After a quantity or a negation they all shrink to de, or d' before a vowel: un kilo de pommes, une bouteille d'eau, je ne mange pas de viande, il n'y a plus de lait. Pronunciation: du has the tight French u (lips rounded), des sounds like "day".

culture.title: Le marché: the open-air market
culture.body: Most French towns and many villages have an open-air market (le marché) once or several times a week, often in the morning on the main square. Farmers and traders sell fruit, vegetables, cheese, meat, fish and bread, and many people do their weekly shopping there. You greet the seller with Bonjour before asking for anything, and you usually let the seller pick and weigh the produce rather than touching it yourself. Markets are also common in Belgium, Switzerland and Québec (where you'll hear marché public).

culture.title: Euros, francs, dollars — and Sundays
culture.body: France, Belgium and Luxembourg pay in euros (un euro, cinquante centimes). Switzerland uses the Swiss franc (le franc suisse, CHF), and Canada the Canadian dollar; in informal Québec French a dollar is often une piasse and a cent une cenne. Many West African francophone countries, such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, use the CFA franc. Opening hours differ too: in France and Switzerland many shops close on Sunday or open only in the morning (bakeries and markets are often open), while in Québec most shops are open on Sundays. Check before you plan a Sunday shop!
